November 9, 2026 — Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 arrive on Anthropic’s IPO roadshow day. How much thinking is worth paying for? On Friday, we asked Jamin Ball what comes next for Anthropic’s IPO . On Monday the roadshow started and Anthropic shipped the long-anticipated next-version of Claude Fable and Mythos . Of course, it is the new top model in the world, taking back Opus 5.5’s #1 spot from Gemini 4 Carbon which had its brief moment in the sun (10 days). Fable comes with a 20% per token price cut… but is more token hungry, as both SemiAnalysis GDPx and Artificial Analysis agree: Fable 5.1 cost $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Fable 5.2 costs $8 and $40 . Yet on GDPx, a benchmark of professional tasks, SemiAnalysis paid $88.15 per task, up from $67.16 . The run logs give a clue. Where Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 would try about 20 test cases, 5.2 sometimes wrote hundreds or thousands and spun up subagents to check its work independently. All that checking helped Fable take first place at 16.4% . You pay for the checks either way. Which effort setting should you put in production? On FrontierCode 2.0, Anthropic reports that Fable at High matched Opus 5.5 at Max for about half the cost per task… but don’t talk about Fable at Max. AI News for 11/07/2026-11/09/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! title: WorkflowArena: Benchmarking Executable Workflow Orchestration in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems rather than as a standalone model operating within a single context. Recent agent harnesses allow the model to instantiate worker agents and to author the executable workflow that coordinates them, shifting the design of system structure from developers to the model at run time. The quality of this organization therefore constitutes a distinct capability, yet existing benchmarks either measure end-to-end task completion or evaluate coordination under structures specified in advance. We formalize this capability as workflow orchestration and introduce WorkflowArena, a benchmark of 145 long-horizon tasks spanning 8 professional domains, from software engineering and formal mathematics to legal analysis and 3D production. Each task specifies an initial workspace and an integrated deliverable composed of interdependent components, which is assessed by a hidden verifier. Agents determine autonomously whether and how to delegate, and all delegation is recorded, enabling joint evaluation of deliverable quality and the organization of the underlying work. Experiments with nine models show that no single configuration performs best across all domains and that systems exhibit distinct delegation strategies: at high effort, Claude models in Claude Code invoke workflows less frequently but with larger worker groups, whereas GPT models in Codex delegate more frequently in smaller units. When the executing model is held fixed on a challenging subset of tasks, workflows authored by Claude Opus 5.5 substantially improve weaker executors, indicating that workflow organization is itself a measurable determinant of task performance.

title: Joi-Bench-Task: Benchmarking Task Coordination in Full-duplex Voice Agents through Interactive Simulation
summary: Full-duplex voice agents enable natural, hands-free interaction, allowing users to refine requests, redirect ongoing work, and seek clarification while the agent is speaking. However, existing voice-agent benchmarks insufficiently isolate coordination between task execution and conversation. We introduce a benchmark that assesses this coordination by examining whether agents track what is being executed, what has been completed, what has been communicated, and what remains to be reported as the conversation evolves. We propose an interactive user simulator that introduces configurable interventions at designated timing in tool execution and spoken result delivery, supporting controllable and reproducible evaluation conditions. We evaluate five leading commercial voice agents along three dimensions: execution responsiveness, coordination under request changes, and coordination under interruptions. Agent evaluations reveal persistent coordination failures. Under request changes, the highest result completion rate is only 55%, indicating difficulty for current voice agents adapting to new requests while preserving earlier obligations. After user interruption, four of the five agents exhibit average information omission rates of at least 23%. These findings highlight task coordination as a central challenge for current voice agents in complex, evolving conversations.

title: Can the Confidence and Decisions of System 1 Models Be Trusted? An Explainability and Perturbation Audit of Jev-Style Decision Models
summary: "System 1" decision models (pioneered by TypeSafe AI's Jev) replace autoregressive text generation with a single forward pass returning typed probability distributions over declared schemas (Choice, Score, Noul). While deployed for low-latency routing and automated triage, their statistical calibration and post-hoc explainability remain uncharacterized. We introduce an open, deterministic audit benchmark evaluating System 1 decision models across calibration under label-preserving perturbations, cross-question interference, and post-hoc attribution faithfulness. Evaluating five open-weight models (0.8B to 27B) alongside generative System 2 baselines -- both single-token logprob scoring and structured JSON/CoT decoding -- across NLI (e-SNLI), adversarial syntactic shortcuts (HANS), synthetic clinical triage (N=900), prompt injection defense (Tensor Trust, N=250), and an 86-case logic-gate trigger suite yields five findings: (1) provider confidence is an exact closed-form dispersion transform (1 - H(p)/ln K on sub-10B models; normalized margin on Clef-27B) rather than empirical accuracy; (2) bundling multiple questions in one request induces directional cross-question interference (11.7% to 22.4% binary flips on Tev1-0.8B, vs. 0.1% to 0.2% on Tev1-4B); (3) System 1 models with >= 4B parameters are faster and better calibrated under syntactic shifts (ECE_w = 0.030 to 0.087) than logprob (0.144) and JSON (0.378) baselines; (4) for prompt-injection defense (N=250), >= 4B models achieve 0.988 to 0.998 AUROC with up to 95.2% recall and 0.0% false alarms at 48 to 60 ms; and (5) single-pass inference makes 512-coalition XAI interactive (1.3 to 3.2 s/input), while KernelSHAP with a logit link (S1-SHAP) mitigates softmax saturation on disjunctive OR gates (89.3% to 100.0% gate recovery vs. 57.1% to 82.1% in prob space; p_adj = 0.004).

title: Socratic-tutor – turns an LLM into a strict personal tutor
story_key: story|title:socratic tutor turns an llm into a strict personal tutor
content_excerpt: A collection of skills for AI agents and chatbots. Each skill is a directory containing a SKILL.md file with instructions for the agent. With a coding agent that supports the common SKILL.md format, copy the skill directory into your agent's skills folder, then ask the agent to use it ("teach me X"). With a plain chatbot, paste the body of the skill's SKILL.md into the chat (or into a custom/system prompt), followed by what you want it to do.

title: Nvidia's AI advantage is moving beyond the GPU
story_key: story|title:nvidia s ai advantage is moving beyond the gpu
content_excerpt: Before this week, the dominant story about Nvidia went something like this: For the first few years of the AI boom, Nvidia was the only source for state-of-the-art GPUs, which became immensely profitable as the industry scaled out. In the last few years, hyperscalers like Amazon and Google have started building their own chips, and Nvidia is no longer the only game in town, leading many investors to wonder how durable its advantage really is. It’s a compelling story, and mostly true. After growing its market cap 10x between the start of 2023 and mid-2025, Nvidia shares have been on a more modest trajectory for the past year, driven by concerns about GPU competition. A new narrative has taken shape since the company’s earnings on Wednesday and investors are starting to realize that Nvidia’s advantage goes far beyond GPUs. As AI’s compute grows into the gigawatt scale, orchestration has become an increasingly complex task. Not surprisingly, Nvidia has built much of the state-of-the-art hardware needed to handle it, giving the company a huge advantage in the systems that surround the GPU even as it sees increased competition on the GPUs themselves. For all the talk of compute as a commodity , it’s still incredibly difficult to operate a mega-scale data center at peak efficiency — and as deployments get bigger and faster, that challenge is only growing. You can see some of this just by looking at the details of what Nvidia is actually selling. The company is currently rolling out its Vera Rubin architecture, which pairs the Rubin GPU with a collection of other units, including the Vera CPU, the Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator, and similar racks for storage and networking. Over the past week, I’ve been talking to folks at Nvidia about what those systems actually do, and the results have been surprising. Like the Rubin GPU, they’re extremely specialized systems, but instead of churning through tokens, they’re making sure everything outside the GPU works as efficiently as possible. If the GPU is the engine, these are the rest of the car. The Vera CPU in particular is focused on the problem of orchestrating data. “Vera is important because there’s only so much memory that you can put in a single server or any sort of compute platform,” Jason Hardy, Nvidia’s VP of storage technology, told me. title: Introducing Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1
summary: Our most advanced models for coding and knowledge work. Their research capabilities also offer an early glimpse of how AI models will contribute to scientific progress.
story_key: model:claude|ver:5.1|title:introducing claude fable 5 1 and claude mythos 5 1
content_excerpt: We’re introducing Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1. They’re the world’s most advanced models for coding and knowledge work—and their research capabilities offer an early glimpse of how AI models will contribute to scientific progress. Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 are the same model, but with different levels of safeguards. Fable 5.1 is generally available, while Mythos 5.1 is available only through our trusted access programs; its safeguards are specifically designed to support work in cybersecurity and the life sciences. Alongside its increased capabilities, Fable 5.1 takes important steps towards addressing the feedback we’ve received from customers on price, data retention, and safeguards. Price . Fable 5.1 will cost an estimated 25% less than Fable 5 for typical workloads, wherever usage is billed by token. This is because we’re reducing our pricing on cache reads (where the model reads inputs that have already been processed and stored). For highly agentic work, the savings will often be much larger—up to approximately 45%. Data retention . Our new system of Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (EFS) gives customers complete privacy (the same as a zero data retention policy) while still being state-of-the-art at preventing adversarial use. EFS works by storing data in cloud infrastructure controlled entirely by the customer, not Anthropic. It will be made available to enterprise customers in phases, beginning later this fall. Until EFS is available, eligible customers will be able to use Fable 5.1 with zero data retention. Safeguards . We’ve improved our safeguards to reduce false positives (where the system flags benign content). In cybersecurity, our newest safeguards block 60% fewer false positives than before. In part, this is because Fable 5.1 can now be used to discover software vulnerabilities—though not to develop exploits for them. In biology, we’ve established an access program, developed in partnership with the US government, to enable access to Claude Mythos 5.1’s advanced biology capabilities. We expect to open enrollment for scientists soon. Claude Fable 5.1 sets a new standard for coding, knowledge work, and long-running problem-solving tasks. The charts below show that Fable 5.1 is capable of much higher performance than its predecessor, Fable 5. And when set to Low or Medium effort, Fable 5.1 achieves results similar to or better than Fable 5’s at a much lower cost. (Note that Fable 5.1 defaults to High effort in Claude Code

title: MIRIX-2.0: Multi-Agent Memory System
summary: Long-term memory lets LLM agents personalize, stay consistent, and reuse what worked before. Parametric memories need training, consolidation can lose details for good, and keeping every record leaves a growing store to search. We present MIRIX-2.0, a multi-agent memory system designed to be practical, accurate, and efficient at once. It is the most accurate of the compared systems on four of five QA benchmarks. It reaches 91.4% on LoCoMo and 72.6% on LongMemEval-S, where it leads the strongest baseline by 14.3 points, and with AutoDream disabled it gains 31.0 and 22.0 points over HyperMem on single-hop and multi-hop document QA. As procedural memory, it yields the highest mean success among the compared memory methods on ALFWorld and WebShop and reaches 49.2% on MetaClaw-Bench, against 44.0% for MetaClaw's skill library. Six typed memory agents keep complete records as the system of record, and a provenance hypergraph indexes episodic and semantic records with n-ary frames that cite their rows. Retrieval runs under explicit budgets, so the evidence a question inspects does not grow with the history. AutoDream merges duplicate anchors outside the write path without rewriting any record, and it distills task sessions into skills. With AutoDream disabled, MIRIX-2.0 answers faster than HyperMem on all five timed benchmarks. It needs no fine-tuning, runs with closed and open models, and its code is public.

title: AMSchem: Automated Schematic Visualization of AMS Circuits via Verifiable Agentic Generation
summary: For decades, the netlist-to-schematic gap has remained a persistent challenge in design automation, especially for analog and mixed-signal (AMS) circuits. Netlists encode connectivity, not visual presentation, making their manual conversion into readable schematics time-consuming and dependent on expert conventions. The same gap leaves LLM-based design tools without structured visual feedback, forcing them to iterate on circuits they cannot see. We present AMSchem, a training-free, verifier-guided agentic framework that automatically generates human-readable schematics from AMS netlists. AMSchem separates circuit-aware visual planning (DrawingIntent) from executable schematic geometry (SchematicIR), and applies localized visual feedback with bounded, revalidated repair patches. Deterministic validators enforce device preservation, pin-net consistency, and geometric correctness throughout. For evaluation, we construct AMSchem-Bench comprising 64 circuits of 12 types. On the 40-circuit schematic subset, AMSchem with gpt-5.5 achieves 85.0\% validity (vs. 32.5\% direct generation). When integrated as a visual feedback module in LLM-based analog design, AMSchem resolves all 13 previously failed cases from AnalogCoder benchmark across five models, substantially improving the success rate. Our dataset and benchmark are available at https://www.amschem.com/benchmark

title: LangSmith BYOC is now available on AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud
summary: LangSmith BYOC now runs on AWS (GA), Azure and Google Cloud (Beta). Your traces, evals, and agent deployments stay in your cloud account while LangChain runs it.
story_key: story|title:langsmith byoc is now available on aws azure and google cloud
content_excerpt: LangSmith Bring Your Own Cloud (BYOC) now runs on AWS (GA), Azure (Beta), and Google Cloud (Beta). Your traces, evals, datasets, prompts, and agent deployments stay in your own cloud account, on the cloud you choose, and LangChain manages the data plane for you, from orchestration and scaling to platform updates. By splitting the control plane and data plane in two, BYOC provides greater flexibily to decide where agents run and where telemetry lives, without taking on the work of running LangSmith. LangChain runs the control plane , which holds auth, org and workspace config, billing metadata, hashed API keys, and static UI assets. You own the data plane , which holds everything sensitive, from traces, prompts, and datasets to experiments, agent deployments, and workspace secrets. An organization can hold several data planes, each in its specific account and region, and each data plane holds its workspaces. This lets you split data planes by region, environment, or business unit. For example, a platform team might run production and staging data planes in separate AWS accounts, while a business unit that standardized on Azure runs its own, separate BYOC deployment on Azure. Each team's traces land in the account that team owns. Until now, teams with strict compliance boundaries deployed and maintained self-hosted LangSmith. This kept their data inside their own boundary, but it took dedicated platform engineers to patch stateful services, configure databases, and run schema migrations. With BYOC, LangChain provisions and operates LangSmith inside your own virtual network. Consider a team running agent applications across several environments. With self-hosted, every update to the execution components meant coordinating downtime and managing custom Helm rollouts in each environment. With BYOC, the data in your data plane stays in your VPC while LangChain handles scaling, schema updates, and runtime dependencies. While self-hosting continues to be a reliable deployment option for customers who require complete control, BYOC provides the best of both worlds for customers who need it. Since we launched BYOC on AWS in August, many teams have chosen to run LangSmith in their own cloud with BYOC. They point to three main benefits: By expanding LangSmith BYOC to Azure and Google Cloud, more teams can get access to this experience while choosing their preferred cloud vendor. title: Zero Mismatch, Simple Async RL: REINFORCE Zero, DeepSeek-V4.1 and Kimi K3.1
summary: Asynchronous RL trains on stale weights. Align rollout and training kernels bit for bit, and unclipped importance sampling corrects that lag. Plus zero-mismatch RL for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Kimi K3.1 and AMD MI355X.
story_key: model:deepseek|ver:4.1|title:zero mismatch simple async rl reinforce zero deepseek v4 1 and kimi k3 1
content_excerpt: Last month, we showed that rollout and training can agree exactly. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash, vLLM and the trainer produced the same logprob for every sampled token, bit for bit, on the fast kernels, with an 8.7% reduction in rollout throughput. An agent skill now does the alignment for each new model. That post was about synchronous RL, which has no weight lag, so zero mismatch removes the only gap between rollout and training. This post is about asynchronous RL, which is faster but off-policy by design. Does zero mismatch still matter there? We answer with a new paper from NVIDIA Research and Inferact (Jian Hu et al.): REINFORCE Zero: Kernel Alignment Unlocks Stable Asynchronous RL with Importance Sampling . All numbers in sections 2 to 4 come from it. In synchronous RL, rollout and training take turns, and each waits for the other. Asynchronous RL runs them at the same time: rollout keeps generating while the learner updates. The price is weight lag . A sample generated with weights version v is trained at version k > v. The gap k − v is not small: REINFORCE Zero runs at lag 2 and 8 on math reasoning, and at lag 64 on agentic tool use. So the learner always trains on samples from an older policy. The standard correction is importance sampling (IS): reweight each token by π / μ, the learner's probability for it divided by the probability the rollout recorded when it sampled it. The question is whether that correction covers the whole gap. π is the learner's computation and μ is the rollout engine's. The second term compares the two at the same weights θv. Weight lag changes smoothly. It telescopes over the most recent updates, and when each update is small it follows a smoothly changing policy trajectory. This is the gap IS is meant to correct. Kernel mismatch fluctuates. It depends on batch composition and numerical execution, so it introduces fluctuations even when rollout and learner use identical weights. Figure 1: Peak-to-median ratio of the importance-weight deviation D3, log scale, for two asynchronous runs on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: REINFORCE Zero with aligned kernels and IS with standard kernels. Source: REINFORCE Zero, Table 2. The REINFORCE Zero paper measures this with D3, the per-update average of w − 1 − log w over tokens, where w is the importance weight. Each token's term is 0 when w = 1 and grows as w moves away from 1. With aligned kernels, D3 peaks at 1.50× its median: unclipped IS keeps the remaining weight-lag mismatch smooth and c
